articleTitle: The use of VSAT to extend the company LAN to all its retail sites
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: Large retail sites such as department stores and supermarkets, and medium sized sites such as bank branches and motor dealerships, now commonly use telecommunications between a number of terminals and printers onsite. Companies have an increasing need to communicate operations information such as sales transactions, stock orders, POS authorisation, pricing tables and business statistics in real time, between the retail branch and the central business. Many of them also see benefit in extending administrative support services such as electronic mail, company news, and access to central databases from headquarters into the branch. The use of local area networks within both headquarters and branch environments is the natural choice, since they give ease of cabling and connection, and support all types of service without restriction in throughput or numbers of terminals. However, interconnection of the HQ to all the branch LANs presents the communications manager with some difficult problems in obtaining satisfactory data throughput and reliability, while keeping costs of transmission, equipment, and network management to a reasonable level. The paper shows how VSAT technology solves many of these problems and provides, in many cases, the best price/performance tradeoff for distributed networking requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evaluation of the protocols within the CODE mesh VSAT network
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: The Co-Operative Data Exchange (CODE) network is a very small aperture terminal (VSAT) system which provides interconnection of local area networks (LANs) at remote sites via satellite. CODE provides both star and mesh capability, dynamically assigning channels on request to the participating sites. The routing function required to ensure the data arrives at the correct end destination is also provided. The CODE hub can provide a data rate of up to 2 Mbps as an outbound signal and the remote sites can respond to the hub (star) or communicate between remote sites (mesh) at 64 kbps. CODE provides the end-user with a standard ethernet interface which provides access to a TCP/IP (transmission control protocol internet protocol) transport service that can support applications such as data dissemination, database interrogation and update, Telnet and e-mail. The CODE technology was initially developed and the CODE network first operated at Ka band frequencies on the European Space Agency's Olympus satellite. The CODE network has now been transferred to the Ku band space segment and also to the alternative Ka band capacity. One example of a Ku band network is the Spanish CODE network which consists of a hub and eight remote sites located at Telecommunication Schools throughout Spain (including the Canary Isles) and uses the HISPASAT space segment to deliver lecture courses from Madrid. The outbound signal is a multimedia signal combining digital voice, video and data with an audio return link. The system has been operational since the end of February 1994.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A protocol enhancer for small-terminal satellite networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: Military communications have long used small satellite terminals to provide communications links. These terminals may be used to interconnect data networks, allowing packet data to be routed between local area and wide area networks connected to the terminals. Many military satellite links operate at modest data rates, and frequently must maintain reasonable performance at high bit error rates. Under such conditions, commercial off the shelf networking equipment has been shown to provide poor performance. Aberdeen University has developed a protocol enhancer which enhances the terrestrial link protocol, providing a considerable gain in performance. The enhancer has recently been used in trials to examine the performance of network applications connected via the enhanced satellite link.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: VSAT interconnection for a wide area diversity system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: Significant improvements in the performance and availability of the service provided by VSAT terminals can be achieved if a small array of Ka-band VSAT terminals, distributed around a city, are interconnected using a metropolitan area network (MAN). Each VSAT is connected to a MAN via a conventional network router. The paper presents a novel approach to the configuration and control of such a network, using the TCP/IP protocol suite, to provide what is commonly known as a wide area diversity network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An adaptive multiple access scheme with dynamic channel allocation for multiservice VSAT networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: We present a multiaccess scheme that, when applied to a VSAT satellite network, could efficiently accommodate a variety of traffic classes and will enable a large number of users to share the satellite channel. The difficulties associated with the introduction of speech are discussed and ways to deal with these are suggested. The optimisation of the protocol's performance is also investigated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: JANUS: one year's experience with a TCP/IP VSAT network
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: JANUS (Joint Academic Network Using Satellites) is an 3-year EC-funded project under the DELTA Programme of DG XIII. Its aim is to build, using a mix of VSAT and terrestrial networking technology, a pilot trans-European operational equivalent of the terrestrial academic Internet networks. The original aim of JANUS was to build a new generation of mesh VSAT technology but after consultation with the EC it was agreed to use available star VSAT technology in a mesh application. The author discusses the first year's operation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: The paper covers the CODENET project, a VSAT network interlinking universities in eastern and western Europe. A one year feasibility study has been completed and the pilot CODENET system is currently under construction. Expansion of the network into the new "Soviet" states and the rest of eastern Europe is foreseen after the completion of the pilot network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An adaptive access protocol for general topology VSAT networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: In recent years there has been a demand for general topology (mesh or hybrid) VSAT networks primarily for Pan European applications in Telematic networks, an infrastructure for desk top video conferencing or for general voice/data communication. One such application proposes the simultaneous mesh interconnection of LAN originated data (packet switched) and PABX originated voice (circuit switched) traffic between different VSAT sites. The authors present a functional description of the adaptive access protocol showing the frame structure, network synchronization and the slot selection procedures for voice and data calls. They also describe the results from a simulation program developed to verify the access protocol and network synchronization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: When the asynchronous transfer mode was adopted in 1987 as the target communications technology for the IBCN, it was recognised that the deployment of an ubiquitous terrestrial infrastructure to support this technology would take many years. A traditional chicken-and-egg situation was in prospect: without a network there would be no user demand; without user demand there would be no network. The satellite, with its broad geographical coverage and relatively fast deployment (and redeployment) capabilities, suggested itself as an obvious transmission gap-filler, but there were difficulties in providing low cost satellite paths at the 155 and 622 Mb/s rates conventionally associated with ATM. In the cell-based ATM environment it could also be expected that source streams, of whatever rate, would contain a proportion, perhaps a high proportion, of empty cells. The prospect of wasting valuable satellite capacity on the transmission of empty cells prompted a change in focus; the gaps between cells became as important as the cells themselves: they cried out to be filled. But a cell-gap filler is, in effect, a cell switch: the concept of a satellite-based ATM switch, an ATM exchange-in-the-sky, presented itself.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integration of VSAT networks into user network environment
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Networking Aspects of Small Terminal Satellite Systems
abstract: The integration of VSAT networks into user environments has some specific impacts caused by the long path delay and by system immanent influences of the transmission path. There are particular demands with the integration into the various protocol environments. The VAST network considered here is about advanced business communication via satellite (ABCS). ABCS is a satellite-based wide area network (WAN) for the networking of local area networks (LANs) and frame relay access devices (FRADs). ABCS is a fully meshed network structure serving up to 30 stations distributed throughout Europe. It offers a transfer rate of up to 4 Mbps with a channel error rate of better than 10/sup -7/. The satellite channel is accessed via the demand-oriented TDMA procedure (time division multiple access) which is communally planned by all stations. When integrating such VSATs into user network environments, the tasks to be solved are the integration of the interface, protocols and the embedding into a standardised network management.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
